Summary assessment
- The FOMC held the funds rate at 5.25–5.50% and continued QT, keeping policy restrictively biased even as inflation has eased. The statement’s line that tighter financial and credit conditions will weigh on activity is corroborated by the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS).
- SLOOS evidence points to broad-based tightening and weaker demand:
  - C&I lending: Banks reported tighter standards and weaker demand for C&I loans (references: Banks REPORT ON C&I loans; Large banks cited deposit outflows, liquidity positions, funding costs, and declines in market value of fixed‑income assets as reasons for tightening).
  - CRE: Banks (including large and foreign banks) reported tighter standards on CRE loans amid concerns about collateral values and the economic outlook, and reduced ease of selling loans (Banks REPORT ON CRE loans; Foreign banks cited credit quality, economic outlook, collateral values, and ease of selling loans).
  - Consumer credit: Banks tightened terms on credit card and auto loans, with approvals more sensitive to FICO scores (Banks TIGHTENING TERMS Credit Card Loans; Banks TIGHTENING TERMS Auto Loans; Banks APPROVAL LIKELIHOOD FICO Score).
- While some banks cited credit quality and economic outlook as reasons for easing at the margin, the net SLOOS signal remains one of tight supply and soft demand across business, CRE, and consumer credit.
- Taken with the Financial Stability Report’s note of system resilience (solid capital/liquidity, stabilized deposits, BTFP backstop) but ongoing vulnerabilities (CRE, leveraged loans, nonbank fragilities, higher term premium), the SLOOS tilt toward tighter credit conditions strengthens the downside skew to growth.

Net effect on tone
- Compared with a mildly negative baseline, SLOOS points to more persistent credit restraint, suggesting a slightly more negative tone.
